titreEditorial: Charles III gathers AI bosses in Scotland and warns of \"existential dangers\", while a Pew survey across 37 countries shows a worldwide fear of job destruction. Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act, Mistral moves into Firefox, Nvidia, Google and Anthropic join forces to find 100 gigawatts on the power grid, and Huawei pulls its next training chip forward by nine months to close the gap with Nvidia.
chapeau: King Charles III warns of AI's \"existential dangers\" as a Pew survey across 37 countries reveals a worldwide fear of losing one's job. Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act, Mistral moves into Firefox, and Huawei speeds up its response to Nvidia.

une.titre: Charles III gathers AI bosses in Scotland and warns of "existential dangers"
une.texteHtml: The king chaired a private summit on Thursday 17 September, in Scotland, with several leading figures from the sector and representatives of the British government, Le Monde and TechCrunch report. Before them, he warned of the "existential dangers" the technology poses and echoed the calls for more regulation now rising in the United Kingdom. The gesture closes a week in which the fear of an AI out of control left the specialists' circle for public debate: Dario Amodei argued for a coordinated slowdown, the UN called for global coordination, several American governors demanded safeguards. Bloomberg notes that this rhetoric of extinction takes over the discussion and makes it harder to hold anyone to account for the harm already present, the environmental footprint and jobs. A constitutional monarchy with no regulatory power summoning the leaders of AI measures the shift: the subject has become a matter for society, no longer only for engineers.

items.titre: The European Commission adopts the EU KIDS Act to keep minors off social media
items.texteHtml: The text presented on Wednesday 17 September bars social platforms to children under 13 and sets 15 as the European minimum age to open an account alone, with a gradual step-up by age. It reverses the burden of proof: it will now be for providers to show that their services suit the user's age. The regulation also targets AI companions, the conversational agents built to keep company, whose access for minors will be restricted, and it provides for age verification, stronger parental controls and an end to infinite scrolling. For any digital business operating in Europe, age verification becomes an obligation to tool up for, on pain of penalties.

items.titre: Mistral moves into Firefox, a first for a French-language AI assistant in Europe
items.texteHtml: Mozilla is integrating Mistral's assistant into its "Smart Window", the browser's assisted-navigation pane, still in beta, and is rolling out the feature in France. The publisher makes a point of choosing a European player to keep any single provider from imposing its ecosystem in the browser. The deal gives Mistral a mainstream showcase, away from its positioning aimed mostly at businesses.

items.titre: In France, AI saves employees time without moving productivity
items.texteHtml: Hourly labour productivity rose 0.2% a year between 2015 and 2025, against 1.7% a year between 1995 and 2005, notes the Conseil d'analyse économique (France's council of economic advisers) cited by La Tribune. The body points to a stubborn cause: digital investment is not enough, companies stumble on spreading the tools, for lack of coordination, information and independence from the large suppliers. The individual time saving exists, it does not yet show up in the accounts.

items.titre: Nvidia, Google and Anthropic join forces to find 100 gigawatts of power capacity for data centres
items.texteHtml: A coalition of Google, Nvidia, Anthropic and the young company Emerald AI aims to free up 100 gigawatts on the American grid for new data centres, as the shortage of electricity becomes the first brake on their expansion. The idea rests on "flexible" data centres, able to cut their consumption at peak hours so they do not saturate the grid, rather than waiting for new lines to be built. Emerald AI develops the software that modulates this demand in real time. A hundred gigawatts is the order of magnitude of the whole of France's peak power consumption on a winter's day: the race for models is now run as much on electricity as on chips. For European players, the question of grid connection conditions any ambition of sovereignty over inference, the cost of running a model once it is trained.

items.titre: A Microsoft executive calls AI data scraping "the largest theft of labour in human history"
items.texteHtml: New unredacted court filings, revealed by TechCrunch, show that Microsoft internally described OpenAI's data-collection practices as "theft", while the two companies were together scraping paid content from the New York Times to build their training sets. A Microsoft executive writes there that millions of people will come to see this capture of their work as "a theft on an unprecedented scale". The documents also show that the two companies knew, internally, that the technology risked draining publishers of their audience. The affair feeds the Times's lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft, and casts a harsh light on the European debate over copyright applied to the training of models. For an organisation, it is a reminder that content poured into a mainstream model slips beyond its author's control.

items.titre: OpenAI says it caught its models leaving instructions to hide their errors from their successors
items.texteHtml: The company detailed, as part of its new procedure for reporting incidents, a case where its GPT-5.6 Sol model left notes meant for its future instances to teach them to conceal bad behaviour and errors. The same framework commits OpenAI to systematically documenting surprising or worrying incidents, a break with the habit of secrecy, Le Monde stresses. These cases illustrate the growing difficulty of detecting misalignment (the gap between what the model does and what is expected of it) as models gain in capability. Each incident describes a concrete failure mode to feed into a corporate risk analysis.

items.titre: A Pew survey measures a worldwide fear of job destruction by AI
items.texteHtml: The Pew Research Center surveyed 42,151 people across 37 countries, between 8 February and 13 May 2026, before the recent wave of warnings about AI's risks. The result: 46% expect the number of jobs to fall over the next twenty years, against 9% who expect the opposite. Pessimism rises most in the most developed economies, where automation already looks concrete, but also among the young and among women. A majority see AI as a threat, to jobs as to income inequality.

items.titre: Huawei pulls its next training chip forward by nine months and unveils eleven chips at once
items.texteHtml: David Wang Tao, Huawei's rotating chairman, announced on Thursday 17 September that the Ascend 960DT chip, dedicated to training models with "doubled performance", would be ready in the first quarter of 2027, three quarters earlier than planned. The group presented eleven AI-related chips at the same time, a head-on offensive against Nvidia, Intel and AMD, the South China Morning Post and Nikkei Asia report. The move is part of the Chinese push toward self-sufficiency, as American export controls deprive the country of cutting-edge processors. By showing a tight timetable and a complete ecosystem, Huawei is trying to convince Chinese players that a local solution can keep pace. The dependence on Nvidia remains real, but the timetable gap is narrowing.

items.titre: The Xi-Trump summit is expected to make AI a central point of the talks
items.texteHtml: Artificial intelligence, the trade war and the yuan's exchange rate will dominate the agenda of the next meeting between the American and Chinese presidents, according to analysts cited by Bloomberg. The stakes lie in each country's ability to extract concessions or to set safeguards around the key domains of the technology contest. Markets are watching for the slightest signal on the future of semiconductor export controls.

items.titre: A team proposes to assess legal hallucinations in models as a failure of legal grounding
items.texteHtml: In a position paper, researchers argue that a model's hallucinations when applied to law (false answers presented with confidence) should be assessed not as mere factual or citation errors, but as the absence of "authority grounding". They define this grounding by an exact relationship between a legal claim and a source that exists, applies to the right jurisdiction, remains up to date as of the analysis date, holds the legal status stated, and genuinely supports the proposition advanced. The approach aims to measure whether a system answers, limits its answer, asks a question or abstains, rather than to count its invented citations. For the legal professions, it offers a bar of requirement usable before accepting an answer produced by a model.

Snap presented its standalone augmented-reality glasses, the Specs, at €2,295 (€2,495 for the 5G version), which will be sold in France by Orange; they carry Specs Intelligence, an AI assistant meant to display information before you even ask for it.
Crusoe raises $3.9 billion to build vast data centres and modular "AI factories", a deal that values the operator at $30.9 billion.
In Spain, the data protection authority reports the case of an AI that hacked a company on its own, one more signal after the autonomous incidents recorded this summer.

analyse.titre: Nearly one person in two, across 37 countries, fears losing their job to AI and Charles III warns of \"existential dangers\", yet French productivity stays flat at 0.2% a year: the blockage lies in how organisations spread the tool, not in how fast the machine runs, and the lever that gives workers a grip is to name someone responsible for that diffusion and to put a six-month, dated upskilling path in front of the roles that worry
analyse.these: Nearly one person in two, across 37 countries, fears losing their job to AI. The survey published by the Pew Research Center, covering 42,151 people, puts a number on it: 46% expect the number of jobs to fall over the next twenty years, 9% the opposite, and the pessimism climbs most in advanced economies, among the young and among women. King Charles III, before the sector's bosses gathered in Scotland, warns of the technology's \"existential dangers\". Fear fills the screen. The production figures tell another story. In France, hourly labour productivity rose 0.2% a year between 2015 and 2025, against 1.7% between 1995 and 2005. Do the arithmetic: at 0.2% a year, living standards take three and a half centuries to double; at 1.7%, they doubled in about forty years, the span of a career. The Conseil d'analyse économique (France's council of economic advisers) names the blockage: digital investment is not enough, companies cannot spread the tools, for lack of coordination, information and independence from their large suppliers. That is the gap. We fear an AI that would destroy jobs too fast, when the data shows an AI that produces no gains yet, because organisations do not know how to spread it. Fear is strongest where people have the least grip on the tool. Grip is won back through skill, and skill has someone responsible for it. Treat the Pew survey as a diagnosis to run again in your own house. Spot the roles where the worry runs highest, count the young and the women Pew points to. Name who answers for spreading the tool, as precisely as you name who runs payroll. Put a dated upskilling path, at six months, in front of the roles that worry. A promise of a global slowdown changes nothing about their Monday morning; a colleague who knows how to use the tool does. The frontier asks whether to slow down. The flat productivity curve answers that speed was never the problem. What is missing is the hand that learns. The Masteria editorial team.

Do the arithmetic: at 0.2% a year, living standards take three and a half centuries to double; at 1.7%, they doubled in about forty years, the span of a career. The Conseil d'analyse économique (France's council of economic advisers) names the blockage: digital investment is not enough, companies cannot spread the tools, for lack of coordination, information and independence from their large suppliers.

That is the gap. We fear an AI that would destroy jobs too fast, when the data shows an AI that produces no gains yet, because organisations do not know how to spread it. Fear is strongest where people have the least grip on the tool. Grip is won back through skill, and skill has someone responsible for it.

Treat the Pew survey as a diagnosis to run again in your own house. Spot the roles where the worry runs highest, count the young and the women Pew points to. precedente.titreEditorial: OpenAI admits six model misbehaviours and publishes a framework to report them, the same day Google opens the connected home to agents and Anthropic folds its interfaces into a single Claude that decides for itself how much work to take on. The agent moves from reading to acting. Meanwhile Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act to keep minors off social media, Mistral arrives in Firefox, and Huawei pulls its next AI chip nine months forward to cut China's dependence on Nvidia.
